title: The shameful myths are the Greeks’ own
source_text: Εἶτα ὡς εἰς τὸ μισεῖν μόνον καὶ ἀπεχθάνεσθαι τῷ κατ᾿ Ἰουδαίους καὶ Χριστιανοὺς λόγῳ ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδεδωκὼς, φησὶν ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι ταῦτ᾿ ἀλληγοροῦσι· λέγει δὲ αἰσχυνομένους ἐπὶ τούτοις καταφεύγειν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀλληγορίαν, εἶπε δ᾿ ἄν τις πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι, εἴπερ αἰσχύνης ἄξια τὰ κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ἐκδοχὴν χρὴ λέγειν μύθων καὶ ἀναπλασμάτων, εἴτε δι᾿ ὑπονοίας γεγραμμένων εἴτε ἄλλως ὁπωσοῦν· ἐπὶ τίνων τοῦτο ἢ ἐπὶ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν χρὴ λέγειν ἱστοριῶν; ἐν αἷς υἱοὶ θεοὶ πατέρας θεοὺς ἐκτέμνουσι καὶ πατέρες θεοὶ υἱοὺς θεοὺς καταπίνουσι, καὶ θεὰ μήτηρ ἀντιδίδωσιν υἱοῦ τῷ πατρὶ „ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε“ λίθον, καὶ πατὴρ θυγατρὶ μίγνυται, καὶ γυνὴ καταδεῖ τὸν ἄνδρα, συνεργοὺς εἰς τοὺς δεσμοὺς παραλαμβάνουσα τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ καταδουμένου καὶ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ, καὶ τί με δεῖ καταλέγειν τὰς περὶ θεῶν ἀτόπους Ἑλλήνων ἱστορίας, αἰσχύνης αὐτόθεν ἀξίας καὶ ἀλληγορουμένας; ὅπου γε ὁ Σολεὺς Χρύσιππος, ὁ τὴν Στοὰν τῶν φιλοσόφων πολλοῖς συγγράμμασι συνετοῖς κεκοσμηκέναι νομιζόμενος, παρερμηνεύει γραφὴν τὴν ἐν Σάμῳ, ἐν ᾗ ἀῤῥητοποιοῦσα ἡ Ἥρα τὸν Δία ἐγέγραπτο, λέγει γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ συγγράμμασιν ὁ σεμνὸς φιλόσοφος ὅτι τοὺς σπερματικοὺς λόγους τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ ὕλη παραδεξαμένη ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῇ εἰς κατακόσμησιν τῶν ὅλων, ὕλη γὰρ ἡ ἐν τῇ κατὰ τὴν Σάμον γραφῇ ἡ Ἥρα καὶ ὁ θεὸς ὁ Ζεύς, καὶ διὰ ταῦτα δὴ ἡμεῖς καὶ διὰ τοὺς τοιούτους μύθους καὶ ἄλλους μυρίους οὐδὲ μέχρι ὀνόματος θέλομεν Δία καλεῖν τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν οὐδ᾿ Ἀπόλλωνα τὸν ἥλιον οὐδ᾿ Ἄρτεμιν τὴν σελήνην· ἀλλὰ καθαρὰν εὐσέβειαν εἰς τὸν δημιουργὸν ἀσκοῦντες καὶ τὰ καλὰ αὐτοῦ δημιουργήματα εὐφημοῦντες οὐδὲ μέχρι ὀνόματος χραίνομεν τὰ θεῖα, ἀποδεχόμενοι τοῦ Πλάτωνος τὸν ἐν Φιλήβῳ λόγον, μὴ βουληθέντος τὴν ἡδονὴν παραδέξασθαι θεόν· „τὸ γὰρ ἐμὸν,“ φησὶ, „δέος, ὦ Πρώταρχε, περὶ τὰ τῶν θεῶν ὀνόματα τοιόνδε ἐστίν,“ ἡμεῖς οὖν ἀληθῶς ἔχομεν „δέος“ περὶ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν καλῶν αὐτοῦ δημιουργημάτων, ὡς μηδὲ προφάσει τροπολογίας μῦθόν τινα παραδέξασθαι ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν νέων.
pass_a_gloss: Then, as having given himself (ἐπιδίδωμι) to hating (μισέω) and being hostile (ἀπεχθάνομαι) to the doctrine (λόγος) against Jews and Christians, he says that the more reasonable (ἐπιεικής comp.) of Jews and Christians allegorize (ἀλληγορέω) these things; he says being ashamed (αἰσχύνομαι) at these they flee (καταφεύγω) to allegory (ἀλληγορία). One might say to him that, if one must call worthy of shame (αἰσχύνη) the things in the first sense (πρώτη ἐκδοχή) of myths (μῦθος) and fabrications (ἀνάπλασμα), whether written through hidden meaning (ὑπόνοια) or otherwise in any way, of which must one say this if not of the Greek stories (ἱστορία)? In which sons, gods, castrate (ἐκτέμνω) fathers, gods; fathers, gods, swallow (καταπίνω) sons, gods; a goddess mother gives in exchange (ἀντιδίδωμι) for her son to the father 'of men and gods' a stone; a father has intercourse (μίγνυμι) with a daughter; a wife binds (καταδέω) the husband, taking as co-workers (συνεργός) for the bonds the brother of the one bound and his daughter. And why must I list (καταλέγω) the absurd (ἄτοπος) stories of the Greeks about gods, worthy of shame on their face (αὐτόθεν) even when allegorized? Since Chrysippus of Soli, thought to have adorned (κοσμέω) the Stoa with many intelligent writings, misinterprets (παρερμηνεύω) the painting (γραφή) at Samos in which Hera was painted doing an unspeakable act (ἀρρητοποιέω) with Zeus; for the solemn (σεμνός, ironic) philosopher says in his writings that matter (ὕλη) having received the seminal principles (σπερματικοὶ λόγοι) of god holds them in itself for the ordering (κατακόσμησις) of the whole; for in the painting at Samos Hera is matter and Zeus is the god. And because of these, and such myths and countless others, we do not wish even as far as the name (οὐδὲ μέχρι ὀνόματος) to call the God over all Zeus, nor the sun Apollo, nor the moon Artemis; but practising (ἀσκέω) pure piety (εὐσέβεια) toward the Creator (δημιουργός) and speaking well of (εὐφημέω) his beautiful creations (δημιούργημα), we do not stain (χραίνω) divine things even by name, accepting Plato's word in the Philebus, he not wishing to accept pleasure (ἡδονή) as a god: 'for my fear (δέος), Protarchus, about the names of the gods is such.' We then truly have 'fear' about the name of God and his beautiful creations, so as not even on pretext (πρόφασις) of figurative reading (τροπολογία) to accept any myth to the harm (βλάβη) of the young.
pass_b_english: Then, like a man who has given himself over to nothing but hatred and hostility toward the teaching of Jews and Christians, he says that “the more reasonable among both Jews and Christians allegorize these things.” He says that “being ashamed of them, they take refuge in allegory.” One might answer him: if myths and fictions, whether written with a hidden meaning or in any other way at all, are to be called shameful when taken in their first sense, to which should this be said to apply if not to the stories of the Greeks? In them sons who are gods castrate fathers who are gods, and fathers who are gods swallow sons who are gods; a goddess mother hands the father “of men and gods” (Homer, Iliad 1.544) a stone in place of her son; a father has intercourse with his daughter; and a wife binds her husband, taking as her helpers in the binding the brother of the one being bound and his daughter (Homer, Iliad 1.399–400).

And why need I list the absurd stories of the Greeks about the gods, which are plainly shameful even when they are allegorized? Why, Chrysippus of Soli, who is thought to have adorned the Stoa of the philosophers with many intelligent writings, gives a false interpretation of the painting at Samos in which Hera was painted doing an unspeakable act with Zeus. For this venerable philosopher says in his writings that matter has received the seminal principles of god and holds them in itself for the ordering of the universe; for in the painting at Samos Hera is matter and Zeus is god.

It is for these reasons, and because of such myths and countless others, that we are unwilling to call the God over all “Zeus” even in name, or the sun “Apollo,” or the moon “Artemis.” Rather, practising pure piety toward the Creator and speaking well of his beautiful works, we do not defile divine things even in their names. In this we accept the words of Plato in the Philebus, where he would not accept pleasure as a goddess: “For my fear, Protarchus,” he says, “concerning the names of the gods is of this kind” (Plato, Philebus 12c). We, then, truly have “fear” concerning the name of God and of his beautiful works, so that we do not accept any myth, even on the pretext of a figurative meaning, to the harm of the young.

choices.choice: μόνον restored: 'given himself over to nothing but hatred' (was 'wholly'); ὡς rendered 'like a man who' rather than 'as if'
conditional reordered so the subject (myths and fictions) is clear; dropped added 'and plain'
λέγει γάρ restored ('For this venerable philosopher says'); σεμνός irony rendered 'venerable'
removed added 'he says' before 'Hera is matter'

'These things' (ταῦτα) are the Genesis narratives Celsus mocked in 4.47. Celsus's words are given in indirect speech in the Greek; quotation marks mark the reported claim. Myth allusions (not cited inline because they are allusions, not quotations): Kronos castrates Ouranos (Hesiod, Theogony 178–182); Kronos swallows his children and Rhea gives him a stone (Theogony 459–491); father with daughter is probably Zeus and Persephone; the binding of Zeus by Hera, Poseidon and Athena is Iliad 1.399–400 (cited inline). 'Father of men and gods' is a recurring Homeric formula; Iliad 1.544 is one instance. 'Seminal principles' renders σπερματικοὶ λόγοι (Stoic term). θεός in the Chrysippus report is the Stoic god and is lowercased. Philebus 12c: Plato's text reads πρὸς τὰ τῶν θεῶν ὀνόματα; Origen has περί. τροπολογία rendered 'figurative meaning' throughout. Review: μόνον ('only') rendered 'nothing but'; ὅπου γε rendered 'Why, ...'; σεμνός (ironic) rendered 'venerable'; the clause 'Hera is matter and Zeus is god' is left without an added 'he says', since the Greek does not mark whether it is Chrysippus's statement or Origen's gloss.
